headline: Bethlehem landfill will close a year early, reshaping New Hampshire waste plans
dek: Casella says its North Country Environmental Services landfill will stop accepting municipal waste on Dec. 31, bringing an earlier transition for host-town services and disposal planning across the state.
body: Casella Waste Systems will stop accepting municipal solid waste at its North Country Environmental Services landfill in Bethlehem on Dec. 31, 2026, moving the facility’s expected end of operations forward by a year. The company disclosed the new date in an Oct. 1 [Form 8-K](https://ir.casella.com/sec-filings/sec-filing/8-k/0000911177-26-000052) filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, saying the decision followed an evaluation of remaining permitted airspace, current and projected fill rates and other operating factors. The filing identifies Dec. 31 as the final day the landfill will accept municipal waste for disposal.

The change does not mean the site disappears at midnight or that all waste services end immediately. It means the landfill will no longer take new municipal solid waste; closure and post-closure obligations will continue under applicable permits and environmental requirements. Casella said the earlier timing will increase landfill amortization expense in the fourth quarter, but the company does not expect the change to materially affect its 2026 quarterly or full-year financial results. Those are the company’s projections, not an independent assessment of the site’s long-term costs.

The regional question is where material will go next. [Waste Dive reported](https://www.wastedive.com/news/casella-mulls-early-landfill-closure-announcement-bethlehem-dalton-new-hampshire/832123/) that the Bethlehem facility serves about 200 New Hampshire communities, as well as contractors and other haulers, according to Casella. The company did not identify a single replacement destination, but Casella Vice President of Communications Jeff Weld told the publication that near-term options exist through the company’s transfer and disposal network and third-party sites. That leaves municipalities and private haulers to determine how those arrangements will affect transportation distances, contract prices and disposal capacity after December.

Bethlehem faces a more direct transition because the landfill has supported local services as well as disposal. In a [February letter to residents](https://www.casella.com/media/sk3izqru/2026-2-19-bethlehem-residents-letter.pdf), the NCES general manager said the facility’s planned 2027 closure would end host-community benefits worth about $1.3 million a year. The letter listed curbside trash and recycling collection, transfer-station operations, property-tax payments, annual host fees, community donations and Household Hazardous Waste Day among the services or payments tied to the landfill. Because the closure is now scheduled for the end of 2026, the town has less time than residents were told to expect when that notice was issued.

The effect will vary by community. [New Hampshire Public Radio, republishing Concord Monitor reporting](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-05/casella-bethlehem-landfill-closing-earlier), said Concord already sends its collected waste to the Wheelabrator waste-to-energy facility in Penacook under a 2024 agreement, rather than hauling it to Bethlehem. Adam Clark, a division manager for Concord General Services, told the outlet that the Bethlehem closure should not affect Concord residents. That example shows why the announcement cannot be translated into one statewide service change: some communities have alternate contracts, while others may rely more directly on the landfill’s capacity or Casella’s transfer network.

The closure also lands in the middle of a long-running debate about landfill regulation and environmental oversight. [NHPR reported](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-05/casella-bethlehem-landfill-closing-earlier) that Casella agreed in January to pay $1.9 million in civil penalties tied to state allegations involving the Bethlehem operation. The reported allegations included placing waste beyond permitted boundaries, mishandling leachate, failing to report facility damage, drilling gas wells through a protective liner and failing to apply required daily cover. Those enforcement matters provide context for the facility’s history, but the company’s Oct. 1 filing attributes the new timetable to capacity and operating considerations; it does not say the penalty caused the closure.

The state’s next disposal options are unsettled. New Hampshire has debated Casella’s proposed Granite State Landfill in Dalton as a possible future source of capacity, while residents and environmental groups have opposed that project. [Waste Dive reported](https://www.wastedive.com/news/casella-mulls-early-landfill-closure-announcement-bethlehem-dalton-new-hampshire/832123/) that the Dalton proposal and a new state law placing a temporary limit on landfill-capacity expansion are part of the broader backdrop to the Bethlehem decision. The policy debate matters because closing an existing facility earlier than expected compresses the time available to approve, build or contract for alternatives.

For now, the firm date is Dec. 31. Casella’s filing establishes when municipal-waste intake ends, but it does not provide a public, community-by-community map of replacement disposal routes or a final schedule for Bethlehem’s host-town services. Local governments, haulers and state regulators will need to settle those questions before the last loads arrive. NorthEast News has not independently reviewed Casella’s permits, municipal contracts or the company’s projected post-closure costs; those documents will be important for measuring the practical and financial effects of the accelerated shutdown.
location: North Country Environmental Services landfill, 581 Trudeau Road, Bethlehem, New Hampshire
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Bethlehem landfill closing early in New Hampshire
seoDescription: Casella will close its North Country Environmental Services landfill in Bethlehem on Dec. 31, 2026, a year earlier than planned.
